There Is a Sound of Abundance of Rain
thair iz uh SOWND uv uh-BUN-duns uv RAYN
n. phr. (Elijah to Ahab on Carmel, 1 Kings 18:41)
Hebrew qōl hamōn haggāshem — qōl, a voice or sound; hāmōn, a multitude, tumult or roar; geshem, the heavy downpour as distinct from the early and latter rains.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The fire has fallen, the prophets of Baal are slain, and the sky over Carmel is still empty after three years and six months without rain. Elijah says to Ahab, Get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain. There was no sound. Elijah then climbs to the top of Carmel, casts himself down with his face between his knees, and sends his servant seven times to look toward the sea until a cloud the size of a man's hand appears. The order of events is the point: the prophet announces the rain before there is any evidence of it, and then prays as though everything depended on the praying. He had the word of the LORD — I will send rain upon the earth — and the word was his warrant to speak and his reason to pray, not an excuse to stop. James makes the episode the church's model of prayer and is careful to add that Elijah was a man subject to like passions as we are, lest the example be dismissed as prophetic privilege. The sound Elijah heard was the promise; the rain that came was the answer; and between the two lay seven refusals to give up.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Abundance, great plenty; an overflowing quantity. Sound, the perception of the ear; a noise. 1 Kings 18:41, the rain announced before any sign of it.

Abundance, great plenty; an overflowing quantity; ample sufficiency.

Sound, that which is heard; a noise; the report of a thing.

Rain, water falling in drops from the clouds.

Hebrew geshem, a heavy rain or downpour; hāmōn, a roar or multitude.

Effectual fervent prayer, James 5:16-18, where Elijah is the instance given.

Key Scripture

1Ki 18:1 — "And it came to pass after many days, that the word of the LORD came to Elijah in the third year, saying, Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth."

1Ki 18:41 — "And Elijah said unto Ahab, Get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain."

1Ki 18:43 — "And said to his servant, Go up now, look toward the sea. And he went up, and looked, and said, There is nothing. And he said, Go again seven times."

Jam 5:17 — "Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months."

Modern Corruption

The verse is made a proof text for naming blessings into existence by confident speech, which reverses its logic; or Elijah's praying is read as redundant beside the promise.

expand to see more

The word-of-faith and name-it-and-claim-it teachers have made this verse a showpiece: Elijah declared what he could not see and it came to pass, therefore the believer's confident declaration creates the outcome. The chapter will not support it. Elijah is not generating a result by speech; he is repeating what God had already told him in verse one of the same chapter, Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth. The sound he heard was a promise given, not a reality summoned. Faith that has a word from God to stand on is the whole of the example, and a declaration with no such word behind it is presumption wearing faith's clothes. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the entry names the word-of-faith formula in order to reject it

The opposite error treats the praying as theatre. If God had promised rain, why send the servant seven times? Because Scripture everywhere joins the decree to the means, and prayer is among the appointed means. Daniel read in Jeremiah that the seventy years were determined and immediately set his face to seek the LORD by prayer and supplications. The doctrine to recover is that a promise is a reason to pray and never a reason to stop, and that the man who prayed until the seventh look was not doubting the word but honouring it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qōl hāmōn geshem, the roar of a downpour — a promise heard before it is seen, and prayed through until it came.

expand to see more

Hebrew qōl, a voice or sound; here a sound no one else could hear.

Hebrew hāmōn, a multitude, tumult, or roaring abundance.

Hebrew geshem, the heavy rain, distinct from yōreh and malqōsh.

The warrant is the word already given in 1 Kings 18:1.

The servant is sent seven times before the cloud appears, 1 Kings 18:43.

Usage

"get thee up, eat and drink; for there is a sound of abundance of rain"

"go again seven times"

"Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are"
